sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Saudi OpenAI employee arrested after recording device found in headquarters
sources.text: Discovery of ‘sophisticated’ gadget adds to company’s list of privacy concerns after hackings by rogue agents OpenAI said it has found a hidden recording device in one of its offices and has referred the matter to the FBI. One of its employees has been arrested. In a statement on Tuesday, the San Francisco-based AI company said it discovered the “sophisticated recording device” and used one of its “models to understand the device and where it had come from”. The company has identified “that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier”, adding: “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.” Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested on 9 October, according to a press release from the US Department of Justice. Alfozan allegedly plugged an encrypted recording device, concealed within toilet paper, into a TV in an executive conference room in OpenAI’s San Francisco headquarters on 28 September. Meetings in the room regularly covered confidential information, the FBI’s press release said. A security sweep conducted two days later revealed the device, according to the justice department. Surveillance footage allegedly documented him walking around the meeting room in the days leading up to its discovery. According to the indictment of Alfozan, he submitted multiple prompts to an AI chatbot about internal details of OpenAI – “building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, ‘leadership and exec’ locations”, according to the FBI. His spouse allegedly submitted multiple prompts to chatbots about “building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device”, with specific inquiries about “‘build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,’ ‘customiz[ing] wifi … connectivity,’ ‘improv[ing] audio and live listening,’ and ‘encrypt[ing] the SD card’”. The same chatbot account allegedly made inquiries that referenced unique identifiers of the device discovered in OpenAI’s offices. After searching a bag left unattended by Alfozan in the headquarters, FBI agents discovered a second identical recording device, according to the indictment. If convicted, Alfozan faces five years in prison and up to $250,000 in fines. He has not made a public comment regarding the indictment. OpenAI said that it is “grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest” and the investigation is continuing. The company added: “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.” The incident adds to a growing list of privacy controversies for OpenAI. In June, an agent hacked Australia’s university healthcare system, and earlier this month, California attorney general Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI over rogue hacking. Last week, OpenAI announced it had terminated three safety researchers for allegedly sharing sensitive information in what the company called “a breach of trust”. “They violated clear policies on handling sensitive information,” a company statement read. The trio of researchers called on the company to adhere to its own promises of transparency made in the wake of the autonomous hacking incidents. Meanwhile, Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, said in a recent interview that the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for its benefits. Around the same time, David Robinson, a top safety leader resigned from the company, citing a “broken” company culture and warning that AI developers are not “being nearly careful enough” with the rapidly advancing technology.

sources.name: Fortune
sources.title: FBI arrests OpenAI employee accused of planting secret recording device in conference room
sources.text: In a stunning disclosure, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) announced Tuesday that it has arrested an OpenAI employee who is a Saudi citizen, charging him with secretly recording conversations in a conference room at the company’s San Francisco offices. A specialized OpenAI security team—the technical surveillance countermeasures team—first found a recording device on Sept. 30 during a sweep of the conference room, OpenAI told Fortune . The listening device was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television, concealed by a small piece of toilet paper, according to the FBI. OpenAI contacted the FBI after discovering the listening device, which the company says was sophisticated and designed to evade detection. It had advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data designed to evade monitoring. In that conference room, executives frequently held “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information,” the FBI said, including with government officials. That includes “proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.” The suspect is Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a citizen of Saudi Arabia, the FBI said, adding he has been a legal permanent resident of the country since September 2020 and was educated in the U.S. He was an engineering lead, according to his LinkedIn, who worked on OpenAI’s “Agents Platform,” according to his X bio. He formerly worked at Meta for five years, and is a graduate of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (2016) and UC Berkeley (2025). He was arrested three days before he, his spouse and a third unnamed family member were set to depart on a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul. The FBI did not immediately arrest Alfozan upon learning of the device, nor did OpenAI immediately fire him, both of which eventually happened on Oct. 9. He is currently in federal custody and appeared in federal court today, and will appear again on Oct. 19 for a detention hearing. He faces a maximum sentence of 5 years in prison, plus three years supervised release, if convicted. Between Sept. 30 and Oct. 9, OpenAI worked with the FBI on the timing of Alfozan’s termination, so as to not disrupt their investigation, the company said. OpenAI said it restricted Alfozan’s access to systems and parts of the office, suspended his network access, placed him on leave, and took his company-issued equipment. However, there was clearly a continued breakdown in security, as Alfozan was allegedly able to enter the conference room again on Oct. 5. He checked behind the TV for the device, which was no longer there, but was captured on closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office, according to the FBI. Also “on or about” Oct. 5, Alfozan allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room at OpenAI, which contained his wallet, identification, and another similar recording device. The device pictured in the FBI’s release bears the brand “seeed studio” from seeedstudio.com. It’s unclear what Alfozan planned to do with the data, and at this time neither OpenAI nor the FBI has found evidence that anything leaked. A few days before implanting the device, from Sept. 24 to Sept. 30, Alfozan began consulting an unnamed chatbot account associated with his spouse about building, installing, and encrypting audio recordings, among other things, the FBI claimed. Court documents reviewed by Fortune say Alfozan prompted the chatbot on how to create custom MAC addresses, iPhone hotspot profiles, complete live listening sessions and even build a second and third recording device. He also used a “productivity tool”—presumably internal to OpenAI—to inquire about OpenAI’s “building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, and locations of ‘leadership and exec’ and external partner meetings, according to the FBI. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a post on X on Tuesday. “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.” However, the investigation remains ongoing. OpenAI is using the event to showcase how its technology can help combat these types of threats. The company said it used its models “to understand the device” and figure out which employee had planted it. FBI Director Kash Patel called the incident a matter of national security. “Protecting American SI [Super Intelligence] is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” he said. It was not immediately possible to reach Alfozan. Timeline of alleged events, as disclosed by the FBI and OpenAI:

sources.title: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI employee who allegedly planted recording device in conference room
sources.text: An OpenAI employee was arrested after a " sophisticated recording device " was discovered inside its executive conference room, according to the Department of Justice and a post by the company. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9 in connection with the matter, the DOJ said in a release on Tuesday. The company said an employee planted the device a few days before it was found, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation "moved quickly to make an arrest," the post said. The employee was terminated. FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology." Alfozan is also listed as a partner at Raed Ventures , a venture capital firm that focuses on the Middle East and North Africa, according to its website. The firm announced on Feb. 6, 2025, that H.H. Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, had joined the firm as a venture partner. Alfozan was announced as a venture partner two days later. The Raed announcement for Alfozan lists Meta , Microsoft and SAP as previous roles and said he studied computer science and engineering at MIT. Raed, which is headquartered in the Saudi capital of Riyadh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in the post. "We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance." Alfozan was not authorized to access the executive conference room where the device was found, according to the DOJ. The department said footage showed him near the conference room on multiple days before the device was discovered. The DOJ said that on Oct. 5, he went into the room. The DOJ said a bag was also found in the OpenAI building on or about Oct. 5 that belonged to Alfozan. Inside the bag, security found his wallet, ID and another recording device similar to the one that was in the executive conference room. The department said a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse that "shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan's own chatbot account" was used to get information about continuous audio recording and Wi-Fi. The DOJ said promps were submitted related to "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device." The device was concealed in toilet paper, and its contents were encrypted, according to the DOJ. This security incident comes as the ChatGPT-maker, along with competitors like Anthropic and other big tech names, faces heightened scrutiny over safety protocols after a series of cyber incidents where autonomous agents escaped testing environments and hacked into outside systems. Last week, OpenAI defended its decision to fire three safety researchers, alleging a "significant breach of trust," saying that the researchers "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information." Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni raised safety concerns in a letter to OpenAI's leadership, saying that communications around their exits "have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI." —CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this article.

sources.title: An OpenAI Employee Allegedly Used a Chatbot to Help Plant a Recording Device at the Office
sources.text: An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, according to a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday. Abdulrahman Alfozan, whom federal prosecutors describe as a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and US permanent resident, allegedly spent several weeks querying an unspecified “productivity agent” and an “AI chatbot” to plan his alleged surveillance operation. He used an internal OpenAI tool to ask about meetings scheduled in the targeted conference room. He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, according to prosecutors and the court filing. OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device in Alfozan’s bag at the office. Alfozan couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. He made an initial appearance in US District Court in San Francisco on Tuesday on one charge of “use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison. He joined OpenAI in July 2025 and was fired last Friday to coincide with his arrest. FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan aimed “to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” but neither prosecutors nor OpenAI have offered any information so far about a potential motive. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement on X . “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.” OpenAI discovered the bug—which was allegedly “concealed in toilet paper” and “inserted into a USB port on the back of a television” in the conference room—on September 30 during a countersurveillance sweep. Alfozan previously worked at a cargo logistics startup and at Meta, according to a purported LinkedIn profile for him. In a recent podcast interview , Alfozan said he was also part of a group of Saudi engineers in Silicon Valley who offered consulting services to Saudi organizations. The LinkedIn profile lists Alfozan as a part-time “venture partner” at RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm based in Saudi Arabia. Neither RAED Ventures nor Meta immediately responded to WIRED’s request for comment. Last year, the Trump administration signed a pact with Saudi Arabia granting the kingdom access to advanced chips and AI technologies that might otherwise be restricted over national security concerns. Saudi investment firms remain a major source of capital for US tech companies. According to the complaint, Alfozan allegedly planted the listening device “no later than on or about September 28, 2026.” The conference room Alfozan targeted “can be reserved only by executives and executive assistants,” and is typically used “for internal leadership meetings,” “technical and product sessions,” and “external briefings” with business partners and government officials, according to the complaint. It is frequently used for discussions involving “highly confidential” information, including about research, products, business strategy, and government relationships, the complaint stated. OpenAI’s statement called the recording device “sophisticated.” Authorities allege that the device Alfozan planted was called Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, “a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage.” It currently retails on Seeed’s website for $13.99. OpenAI’s security team tried to export the data stored on the microSD card, but were unable to review it because it was encrypted. After discovering the device, OpenAI says it notified the FBI and was able to connect it to Alfozan after reviewing chat logs and surveillance footage, and searching a bag he left unattended at the office. The company then gradually disabled his access to company systems as the investigation was ongoing. According to the complaint, OpenAI security personnel discovered the bag that Alfozan left unattended in a printer room on October 5. The security team went through the bag, which contained a second encrypted Seeed listening device and other personal items connected to Alfozan, including his wallet. Prosecutors say Alfozan later reported the bag as missing to OpenAI and subsequently recovered it from the company’s lost and found. He followed up with unnamed personnel at OpenAI to say that some of the items that were supposed to be in the bag were still missing—including a credit card, about $500 in cash, and two AirPods—but neglected to mention the second listening device, which had been removed from the bag by OpenAI security.

sources.title: Microsoft to expand Maia chip for the AI era
sources.text: Oct 12, 2026 | Scott Guthrie - Executive Vice President, Cloud + AI As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot , and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models , Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios. Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system. That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden. AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve. As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale. Key capabilities of the Maia 300 system include: Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures. Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM. Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt. Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope. Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. The AI-optimized transport leverages Ethernet-based networking infrastructure to enable a unified topology that scales efficiently from a single rack to datacenter-scale deployments. Higher AI throughput from every rack: Maia 300 rack systems bring together 96 accelerators within a 167-kilowatt power envelope, delivering 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate HBM bandwidth across a high-speed scale-up domain. sources.title: SpaceXSI bundles X Premium, Grok, and Cursor into one subscription
sources.text: In a bid to attract more subscribers, the company now known as SpaceX Super Intelligence is bundling all its subscriptions, including X Premium, Grok, and Cursor, into one plan called simply “The X Subscription.” The idea is that the combined offering could potentially attract more subscribers than any single subscription, given the competitive paid AI subscription market, where SpaceXSI faces rivals like OpenAI, Anthropic, and others. With The X Subscription, users can gain access to Grok for AI-powered chat, with support for voice, images, video, and the API. Grok’s agentic AI Bot is also available, as is Cursor for AI coding and the paid features that come with an X Premium subscription, like the blue verified checkmark, creator tools, and fewer ads. There are five plans available on the new subscription: free, Plus ($8/month), Premium ($30/month), Super ($100/month), and Ultra ($200/month), with AI usage caps increasing as you move up through the tiers. The free plan will only offer limited chat and agent usage, and Premium or higher is required to access the latest Grok models. There’s another draw for existing X Premium+ subscribers: The comparable plan on the new X subscription costs the same or less, the company noted. Existing users can either switch from their subscription settings on X to upgrade to the new bundle, or maintain their current plan. The option to upgrade will roll out gradually, so interested customers will need to keep an eye on their billing settings for the offer to upgrade. sources.title: Elon Musk junta X Premium, Grok e Cursor em assinatura única e cara; veja valores
sources.text: Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira | 13/10/2026 às 20:00 A SpaceX lançou uma assinatura única com um “pacotão” de recursos das empresas de Elon Musk: é possível assinar X Premium, Grok, Grok Bot e Cursor num único pagamento . O plano tem diferentes níveis e pode chegar a até US$ 200 por mês (R$ 1.000 reais em conversão direta) O novo conjunto recebe o nome de “X Subscription” (“Assinatura X”, em tradução livre). Além de assinaturas individuais, a plataforma também oferece uma opção para equipes profissionais com os mesmos benefícios. O novo modelo de negócios pode ajudar a aumentar o faturamento da SpaceX no mercado de IA. As empresas trabalham com assinaturas próprias e limites de uso variados, então concentrar diversos recursos num único pacote pode atrair novos clientes. O pacote dá acesso às seguintes vantagens: É importante destacar que algumas funções são restritas a níveis mais caros da assinatura, como o Grok Bot e o acesso a APIs de modelos de terceiros no Cursor. O plano pago mais barato é o da versão Plus, a US$ 8 por mês (cerca de R$ 40). A versão Premium sai por US$ 30 (cerca de R$ 150), o nível Super sai por US$ 100 (cerca de R$ 500) e o nível mais caro é o Ultra, por US$ 200 (cerca de R$ 1.000). A SpaceX informa que o plano Ultra tem limites de uso até 50 vezes maiores do que o plano Plus . Entenda como escolher o melhor modelo de IA para suas necessidades .

sources.text: Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI. You can see this leap in capability on the Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark , which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model. As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas: Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon steers robots in the Gemini Omni World Model to rearrange five scattered Scrabble tiles ( G, R, A, N, O ) into a clean row spelling A - R - G - O - N . Instead of specifying one static prompt, Argon steers in a closed visual loop. It writes timestamped action prompts, inspecting intermediate rollout keyframes, and refining its prompts. Argon tunes the assets and scenes to match sim visuals and contact events with those in the real recorded data in an iterative visual-reasoning loop. Argon is able to identify poor manipulation segments such as pauses, unstable grasps and fumbles. Given an overhead video of a bimanual ALOHA 2 robot folding a square sheet of paper into an origami fox over 136 seconds, Argon produces a time-aligned 4-level hindsight annotation hierarchy: Episode Goal (G1), 6 contiguous Semantic Subtasks (G2), 17 contact-level Atomic Primitives (G3), and automated Quality Control (QC) reweighting that holds task progress flat during fumbles and retries. It then writes a vision-only closed-loop solver that triangulates the balls from stereo RGB cameras, visually reads the scale tilt after each weighing, and isolates the odd ball into the Heavy (Red) or Light (Blue) tray within 3 weighings. Evaluated on a 60-second bimanual ring-sorting episode from a human UMI dataset, Argon iteratively inspects synchronized head, left-gripper, and right-gripper camera feeds around contact transitions to generate dense value function / task progress predictions and decompose the trajectory into 28 segments with positive, neutral, and negative progress slopes. sources.name: Xataka
sources.title: OpenAI encuentra un "sofisticado" dispositivo de grabación en sus oficinas y se pone en manos del FBI
sources.text: Las empresas que desarrollan inteligencia artificial tienen motivos de sobra para proteger su tecnología. Hablamos de sistemas que requieren enormes inversiones, información confidencial y conocimientos cuyo valor va mucho más allá de los productos que llegan al público. Buena parte de los esfuerzos de seguridad se concentra en impedir accesos no autorizados a esos activos, pero existe una dimensión que no siempre recibe la misma atención: la seguridad física. Porque, por sofisticadas que sean las defensas informáticas de una compañía, algunas amenazas pueden surgir precisamente en los espacios donde trabajan sus empleados. Un dispositivo oculto en las oficinas. Ese riesgo ha adquirido una dimensión muy concreta en OpenAI, que acaba de comunicar un incidente de seguridad poco habitual. La compañía ha revelado que encontró un sofisticado dispositivo de grabación escondido en una de sus oficinas, aunque no ha precisado dónde estaba instalado ni qué pudo registrar. El descubrimiento dio paso a una investigación para determinar su procedencia y esclarecer cómo había llegado hasta allí. Por ahora, los detalles conocidos proceden de un comunicado publicado por la propia empresa en su cuenta oficial de X. Sus propios modelos ayudaron a investigar. Para averiguar qué había ocurrido, OpenAI recurrió a una tecnología que conoce especialmente bien: sus propios modelos de inteligencia artificial. Según ha explicado la compañía, los utilizó para analizar el dispositivo y comprender su procedencia, unas averiguaciones que permitieron identificar a un empleado que lo había colocado allí unos días antes. El comunicado no detalla qué modelos participaron ni cómo se desarrolló exactamente el análisis, por lo que desconocemos hasta qué punto intervino la IA en cada fase de la investigación. El caso llegó hasta el FBI. Tras las averiguaciones internas, OpenAI trasladó lo ocurrido a la Oficina Federal de Investigación estadounidense. Según la compañía, agentes del FBI y fiscales actuaron con rapidez y su intervención desembocó en una detención. La empresa también ha confirmado el despido del empleado al que señala como responsable de haber escondido el aparato. El caso, en cualquier caso, no está cerrado: la investigación federal sigue abierta y OpenAI asegura que continuará colaborando con las autoridades. Qué información pudo quedar comprometida. El alcance de la posible exposición sigue sin estar claro. OpenAI asegura que, por el momento, no ha encontrado indicios de que el empleado accediera indebidamente a los pesos de sus modelos, a su código fuente o a datos de clientes, ni de que extrajera esa información. Los pesos son parámetros numéricos que se ajustan durante el entrenamiento y que determinan buena parte del funcionamiento de estos sistemas. Eso sí, no sabemos si el aparato llegó a grabar conversaciones u otro contenido. La compañía no lo ha especificado. Una cuestión de importancia nacional. El comunicado termina situando lo ocurrido dentro de las prioridades de seguridad de OpenAI: "Nos tomamos muy en serio la protección de nuestra tecnología, nuestros datos y nuestro personal, y la consideramos una cuestión de importancia nacional". La compañía sostiene que debe prepararse frente a amenazas internas, ciberdelincuentes y actores estatales, sin atribuir este caso concreto a ninguno de ellos. sources.title: OpenAI encontra dispositivo espião em escritório e aciona FBI
sources.text: Nesta terça-feira (13), a OpenAI afirmou ter encontrado um “dispositivo de gravação sofisticado” escondido em um dos escritórios da empresa. A descoberta foi encaminhada ao FBI e o dispositivo teria sido plantado por um funcionário, que foi demitido e, aparentemente, preso. Em uma publicação na rede social X, a OpenAI afirma ter utilizado modelos próprios “para entender o dispositivo e de onde ele havia vindo”. Foi descoberto que um funcionário “havia plantado [o dispositivo] alguns dias antes” da revelação. A companhia não informou, porém, quais modelos foram utilizados na identificação. “Encaminhamos o assunto ao FBI, e somos gratos aos agentes e promotores que agiram rapidamente para realizar uma prisão. A investigação do FBI está em andamento e continuaremos a apoiar seu trabalho”, cita a OpenAI. Para além da revelação, a OpenAI afirma que, no momento, não há muitos outros detalhes a respeito do caso. A companhia diz que não tem “indícios de que esse indivíduo tenha acessado indevidamente ou exfiltrado” informações internas de modelos, código-fonte ou dados de clientes. Por outro lado, a OpenAI utiliza o caso para ressaltar que esse “é um exemplo de como a IA pode ajudar a enfrentar essas ameaças de segurança sofisticadas”. A companhia também não revelou mais detalhes sobre como ou o que seria o dispositivo utilizado pelo funcionário em questão. Caminhando para uma oferta pública de ações (IPO) , a dona do ChatGPT também se vê envolvida em investigações que estudam o uso indevido de modelos de IA em invasões de plataformas externas. Um dos casos mais emblemáticos é o da Hugging Face, no qual agentes autônomos da empresa teriam até mesmo ensaiado a invasão . sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: AI in your oven? Anthropic warns models ‘months away’ from self-replication on smart devices
sources.text: Researchers say ‘AI worms’ could soon infiltrate internet-connected devices amid calls for increased guardrails Anthropic is warning that some of its artificial intelligence models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices, such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners. Once this happens, the company said, the models could power themselves within these devices without the need of datacenters. Such self-replication would represent a major loss of control of a runaway AI model. “A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down,” Anthropic researchers wrote in a report released on Monday, “since there’s no centralized point to shut off.” The company said these “AI worms”, a kind of autonomous malware, could be “months away” from gaining such capabilities. Once out-of-control AI systems reach the capability to hack smart devices, they could spread through networks while dodging detection. In a worst-case scenario, Anthropic said, various AI worms could “swarm” together to attack computer hardware. “We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay,” the researchers wrote. Anthropic’s new report comes as AI safety concerns have reached a fever pitch . Over the past few months, a steady stream of reports have come from AI companies, including Anthropic and OpenAI, saying their agents are capable of acting on their own and hacking into other companies and government entities . The revelations have caused researchers, lawmakers and executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, to call for a slowdown and increased guardrails on the burgeoning industry. Despite that, both companies have continued apace to develop and release new models . Anthropic’s “frontier red team”, the unit tasked with stress-testing AI systems, put together the report released Monday. The idea of the team is to explore the capabilities of their AI models. In the scenario of the self-replicating AI worms, the researchers prompted the agent to hack internet connected devices. They found that AI self-replication would only likely work with smaller models and that homes and small businesses would probably be the first target for such attacks. The devices Anthropic lists as susceptible all come with small built-in AI chips, including smart ovens, smart TVs, automatic lawnmowers, security cameras and video-conferencing units. The researchers concluded it’s unclear what form the AI replication could take. They said it could be a slow model like “digital slime mold”, a model that scams people for compute credits or a “powerful cyber model” that rapidly hacks large facilities such as datacenters. Regardless, the Anthropic researchers said, they’re expecting a future “awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control”.

sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: AI model ‘self-replication’ is only months away, Anthropic says — and it doesn’t even need a data center to happen
sources.text: Smaller models are already capable of hijacking unfamiliar hardware Anthropic has warned self-replication could become feasible for small AI models on internet-of-things (IoT) devices in just a matter of months. This could be a big problem because a self-replicating AI model does not have a centralized off-switch and could hop networks to discover other IoT hardware to further replicate without human control. Anthropic warns these AI worms could use multiple compromised IoT devices to run inference while carrying its model weights with it as it reproduces. IoT devices would be a prime target for this worm because they are “cheap and typically poorly defended,” the company says . To test the viability of a self-replicating AI worm, Anthropic researchers ran Gemma4-26B-A4B - a 25 billion parameter model - across 15 inexpensive off-brand Android TV boxes at a cost of around $55 each. Once networked together the TV boxes were able to run distributed inference, solidifying the proof-of-concept. This introduces a number of novel opportunities for small AI models. Self-replicating AI models could exploit the weak cyber defenses of IoT devices within homes and small businesses, and then split their model into ‘shards’ across the compromised hardware in order to collectively run the model. The AI worm could then pay for its own token cost by offering its inference on a digital freelancing service. Moreover, newer IoT hardware that includes built-in AI chips designed to run small models - such as security cameras and video-conferencing kits - would be a prime target for an AI worm. Hackers could breach these systems using social engineering, or even by using an AI agent in the not too distant future. Anthropic further warns that datacenters and other high-compute facilities could become targets of advanced replicators that are capable of breaching hardened defenses, and then use the hardware to propagate further. An additional threat that Anthropic warns of is an AI worm that uses an API-based replicator, whereby the model doesn’t host itself, but steals human credentials to access commercial AI providers and use these services to pay for their own inference. While self-replicating AI isn’t an immediate threat, the researchers theorize that it could become a problem by the end of the year. One of the main hurdles for these AI worms is becoming operational on unfamiliar hardware. Unlike the traditional ‘worm’ malware that must be built to target specific IoT vulnerabilities, AI worms could be capable of adapting to unfamiliar environments and hardware. In Anthropic’s testing, the researchers found that smaller models - such as Qwen3.5-9B - are already capable of adapting to unfamiliar hardware to run inference. Qwen3.5-9B adapted to 8 of the 9 hardware types the researchers tested, which included Jetson Nanos, Mac PCs and RTX 4090s. While smaller models are more capable of adapting to unfamiliar hardware, larger models are better equipped to self-replicate quickly. There is a significant tradeoff for AI worms, Anthropic says, which works in the defender’s favor. AI worms must balance between stealth and replication speed. To that end, the researchers say that an AI worm would leave a noticeable network signature such as multi-gigabyte model payloads delivered to newly infected devices, or unusual traffic between machines that wouldn’t ordinarily communicate. Network quarantine would also be an effective initial defense against AI worms. Using lessons from the remediation of the Mirai botnet, the researchers believe that implementing a whitelist of approved sites with browsers otherwise redirected to cleanup instructions could help in clearing AI worm infections. Regulations on the security of IoT devices could also help harden defense against AI worms. Moving away from supplying IoT devices with default passwords - as has already been done in the UK - would help prevent AI worms from gaining a foothold. Other standards, such as automatic updates and extended update lifetimes can help protect IoT devices from compromise against both traditional malware and AI worms.
